meta.description: Yes — the thought is genuinely Blaise Pascal's, from his 1656 Sixteenth Provincial Letter. But this exact English wording is a modern paraphrase, not his own words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have made this longer than usual because I have not had time to make it shorter'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Pascal — he wrote it in French in 1656. This popular English line is a modern paraphrase, not a documented translation.

answer.label: Genuinely Blaise Pascal — but this English is a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: Pascal really did write this — in French — in the Sixteenth of his Lettres provinciales, dated 4 December 1656 (published 1657): “Je n’ai fait celle-ci plus longue que parce que je n’ai pas eu le loisir de la faire plus courte.” The idea and the original sentence are firmly his, as Quote Investigator documents. But the crisp English line quoted here is a modern floating paraphrase; it does not match his earliest 1658 English translation or any specific documented rendering.

trail: Quote Investigator traces the earliest English instance to a 1658 London translation of Pascal’s French, and debunks the Mark Twain connection.

source.excerptNote: Pascal’s original line, closing the Sixteenth Provincial Letter (4 December 1656). Literally: “I have made this one longer only because I have not had the leisure to make it shorter.” The popular “I have made this longer than usual…” wording is a later, smoother paraphrase.
source.rightsNote: Pascal’s original French sentence appears in the Lettres provinciales (1657), and the first English translation was printed in London in 1658 — both far older than 1931 and unquestionably in the public domain. The specific modern English wording shown is an untraceable paraphrase of that same public-domain sentence rather than a distinct copyrighted translation.

author.name: Blaise Pascal
author.heading: About Blaise Pascal
author.bio: Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor and religious philosopher, a founder of probability theory and projective geometry. Under the pseudonym Louis de Montalte he wrote the Lettres provinciales (1656–57), a series of polemical open letters defending the Jansenist Antoine Arnauld and attacking Jesuit casuistry. Admired for their wit and prose, the letters are where his famous apology for a long letter appears.

misattribution.heading: Who it's wrongly credited to
misattribution.intro: The sentiment is genuinely Pascal’s, but the pithy English line gets pinned on a rotating cast of famous names — and the wording itself is not actually his.

items.why: Routinely credited to Twain online, but Quote Investigator found no evidence he ever used it.

items.who: Cicero, T. S. Eliot, Voltaire, Goethe
items.why: Various eloquent names get attached with no source; none predates Pascal’s 1656 letter for this specific remark.

Franklin wrote a genuinely similar apology in 1750 (“I have already made this paper too long, for which I must crave pardon, not having now time to make it shorter”), which is often blurred together with Pascal’s line, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest known form of this quip is Pascal’s French sentence in the Sixteenth Provincial Letter (1656); the popular English — and every celebrity credited with it — came later, as Quote Investigator shows.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Pascal added the line as a wry closing apology to the sixteenth of his Provincial Letters — anonymous pamphlets in the bitter Jansenist–Jesuit dispute of the 1650s. The joke lands because it is true: cutting prose to its essentials takes more time and craft than letting it run long.

Because the thought is so universally felt by writers, the English paraphrase has drifted freely across centuries and been re-credited to nearly every famous wit — a textbook case of a real idea outrunning its real author.
context.pull: Brevity is the expensive option — and Pascal said so first.
